title: Git Fundamentals: Track, Commit, and Publish Your Work
description: Understand Git's three local areas, record focused changes as commits, connect a local repository to a remote, publish a branch, and keep generated or secret files out of version control.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between the working tree, staging area, local repository, and remote repository.
Use git init, git status, git add, git commit, git remote, and git push in a deliberate workflow.
Explain why staging allows one commit to contain selected changes rather than every changed file.
Create a useful .gitignore and identify files that should not be committed.
Read the outcome of Git commands and recover from common beginner mistakes without deleting work.
Publish a small project to a remote repository using a focused commit history.
Use stash, aliases and amend with an explicit understanding of what is local and what has been shared.
Write a readable Markdown README and verify the configured GitHub Pages publishing path and deployment result.

blocks.text: Git records the history of a project

Git is a distributed version control system. It records snapshots of project content as commits, so you can inspect changes, compare versions, create branches, and collaborate without relying on folders such as final, final-2, or final-really-final. A commit is not simply an automatic backup of every file on your computer; it records the content selected for that commit along with metadata such as its author, message, and parent history.

blocks.title: Track the path a change takes
blocks.text: Think in three local areas: the working tree contains your current files, the staging area records what you intend to include in the next commit, and the local repository stores commits. A remote repository is a separate repository hosted elsewhere. Most everyday Git commands move changes or references between these areas.
Working tree, staging area, repository, remote

items: Working tree: the files you are currently editing in your checkout.
Staging area (index): the exact content prepared for the next commit.
Local repository: the commits and references stored in your local .git directory.
Remote repository: a named remote copy, commonly hosted on GitHub or GitLab, used to exchange commits with other machines or collaborators.

blocks.text: A basic local workflow

Run Git commands from the project directory. If the folder is not already a repository, initialize it; inspect the current state; stage only the changes meant for the next logical checkpoint; then commit them with a message describing the intent. Use status frequently—it is a report of what Git sees, and is safer than guessing what the next command will include.

blocks.code:
git init
git status
git add index.html src/styles.css
git status
git commit -m "feat: add responsive landing page"
git log --oneline

steps.title: Initialize a repository
steps.explanation: git init creates a local repository in the current directory if one is not already present. Do not run it blindly inside a directory that already belongs to another repository.

steps.title: Inspect before staging
steps.explanation: git status shows modified, untracked, staged, and branch information. Use it to confirm which files Git knows about before choosing what to commit.

steps.title: Choose the exact changes for the commit
steps.explanation: git add places the named files' current content into the staging area. A second status call shows what will be included; staging a file again updates its staged snapshot.

steps.title: Create a permanent local checkpoint
steps.explanation: git commit records staged content in the local repository. The message summarizes the change's purpose; the example uses a conventional prefix and a specific description.

steps.title: Inspect the resulting history
steps.explanation: git log --oneline displays a compact commit history. Each commit represents a checkpoint you can later inspect or compare.

blocks.text: Why staging is useful

Imagine changing three files: one fixes a bug, one adds a feature, and one contains an unfinished experiment. Staging lets you commit the complete bug fix without accidentally including the unfinished experiment. The staging area is the boundary between everything you changed locally and the exact snapshot you want to record next.
Use .gitignore to exclude local or generated files

A .gitignore file tells Git which untracked paths to ignore. Common entries include installed dependency directories, build output, local environment files containing secrets, and editor operating-system artifacts. Ignore rules do not remove a file that is already tracked; to stop tracking it without deleting the local file, you need an explicit index update. Never commit passwords, API tokens, private keys, or production secrets.
Read .gitignore patterns precisely

items: A line starting with `#` is a comment. To match a filename that starts with `#`, escape the leading character as `\#`.
`*.log` matches names ending in `.log`; one `*` does not cross a `/`. A pattern without a slash can match at any directory depth.
`build-[0-9].log` uses a character range: the bracket expression matches one character.
`folder/` matches a directory named `folder` and its contents; the trailing slash makes the pattern directory-specific.

`!` negates an earlier pattern. `.env.*` followed by `!.env.example` ignores environment variants while keeping the example file. However, Git cannot re-include a child if an excluded parent directory prevents Git from traversing it.
When several patterns match the same path, the last matching pattern decides whether it is ignored. Keep exceptions near the broader rule.

blocks.text: Connect to GitHub or GitLab and push

A local commit exists only in your local repository until you exchange it with a remote. Add a remote URL under a name such as origin, inspect the configured URL, and push the branch. On the first push, -u records the upstream relationship so future pushes and pulls can use the shorter branch name. Authentication is separate from Git's commit model; use the host's supported authentication method and never put a personal access token in a repository URL committed to source control.

blocks.code:
git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/PROJECT.git
git remote -v
git branch --show-current
git push -u origin HEAD

steps.title: Add the remote under a memorable name
steps.explanation: origin is only a conventional name. Replace the sample URL with the real repository URL. If origin already exists, inspect it rather than adding it a second time.

steps.title: Verify the remote
steps.explanation: git remote -v lists the fetch and push URLs. This helps catch a wrong repository destination before publishing anything.

steps.title: Confirm the current branch
steps.explanation: Check that the checked-out branch is the intended branch to publish. If the team requires review before integration, create/use a feature branch and open a pull request instead of pushing directly to a protected default branch.

steps.title: Publish local commits
steps.explanation: After confirming the current branch and team policy, `git push -u origin HEAD` publishes the checked-out branch under the same name on origin and sets upstream tracking. It does not mean 'push main' unless you are currently on main; do not bypass a required PR workflow.

blocks.text: Write focused commit messages

A good commit is a small, coherent checkpoint that can be described in one sentence. Messages such as "fix: handle empty search results" or "docs: explain local setup" help teammates scan history. A message such as "changes" does not explain intent. Avoid mixing unrelated feature work, dependency upgrades, content rewrites, and formatting in one very large commit when it can reasonably be split.
Common beginner mistakes and safe recovery

items: Forgetting to stage a file: inspect git status, then git add the intended path and make the commit.
Staging too much with git add .: inspect the staged diff with git diff --cached and unstage unintended paths before committing.
Trying to commit when nothing is staged: use status to see whether files are unchanged, unstaged, or ignored.
Pushing before setting a remote or upstream: inspect git remote -v and git branch -vv, then configure the intended remote/branch.

Accidentally staging a secret: unstage it and make sure the secret is not committed. If a secret has already been pushed, removing the file is not enough—rotate/revoke the credential and follow the host's incident guidance.

blocks.text: Stash, amend, and aliases: three tools with different scope

Use stash when you need to temporarily set aside uncommitted work without creating a commit. `git stash apply` reapplies a saved change and keeps the stash entry; `git stash pop` applies it and removes the entry if successful. By default, untracked files are not included unless you pass `-u`. `git commit --amend` recreates the latest commit, changing its hash and possibly its message; use it for a local, unpublished commit unless the team explicitly coordinates a rewrite. Git aliases are local configuration shortcuts: a `--global` alias applies to your user account on this machine and is not shared automatically with the repository.

blocks.code:
git status
git stash push -u -m "wip: navbar"
git stash list
git stash apply stash@{0}
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate"
git st
git lg
# Only amend a local commit that has not been shared
git commit --amend -m "fix: describe the updated change"

steps.title: Check the current state
steps.explanation: Read git status before moving work. Stash is for uncommitted changes, not a replacement for a meaningful checkpoint commit.

steps.title: Save work without committing it
steps.explanation: The -u flag includes untracked files. The message helps identify the saved work later. Avoid stashing files that contain secrets you do not want to handle indirectly.

steps.title: List and reapply a stash
steps.explanation: git stash list shows stored entries. apply replays the selected changes but keeps the stash entry, which can be useful until you confirm the work is restored correctly.

steps.title: Define shortcuts for this user
steps.explanation: The --global aliases persist in your user configuration on this machine. They do not automatically become part of a teammate's Git configuration.

steps.title: Amend only unpublished history
steps.explanation: --amend creates a replacement commit with a different hash. Do not amend a commit already pushed to a shared branch without explicit team coordination.

items: Use a README to explain what a repository does, how to install dependencies, how to run checks, and how to contribute.
GitHub Pages can publish a static site from a configured branch or a GitHub Actions workflow; verify the source and base-path settings before publishing.
Review repository visibility, collaborator permissions, branch protection, and required checks deliberately; grant only the access each contributor needs.
A .gitignore rule does not remove a tracked secret or erase it from history. If a credential was exposed, rotate or revoke it; removing the file alone is not enough.

Write README content in Markdown: use headings to define hierarchy, fenced code blocks for commands, and links for supporting documentation. Preview the rendered file and keep instructions reproducible and free of secrets.

blocks.text: Write a README that someone can follow

A README is the project's entry point. It should explain the app's purpose, required tools, reproducible setup and verification commands, contribution workflow, and actual deployment constraints. Do not copy commands or versions from another project without checking them.

blocks.code:
# Project Name

A short description of the problem this project solves and who it is for.

## Features
- Summarize the main user-facing capabilities.
- Link to a screenshot or demo when it helps explain a feature.

## Technology
List the framework, key tools, and important version requirements.

## Requirements
- Node.js 22
- npm 11.21.1

## Install and run
```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Checks
```bash
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
```

## Contributing
Describe the branch, pull-request, and review workflow.

## Deployment
Document the configured host, base path, and where deployment status is reported.

## License
Name the chosen license or state that licensing is not yet defined.

## Credits
Link collaborators or third-party assets when appropriate.

steps.title: Explain the purpose and features
steps.explanation: The title, short description, features, and technology stack tell a reader what the repository is for before they run anything.

steps.title: State prerequisites
steps.explanation: List only the tool versions and dependencies the project actually requires.

steps.title: Give reproducible setup commands
steps.explanation: Commands should match the project's lockfile and package scripts rather than remain generic placeholders.

steps.title: Document checks before review
steps.explanation: List the real checks the team runs before a pull request or release.

steps.title: Document contribution and deployment
steps.explanation: Describe contribution/review and the actual hosting configuration. Name a license only after one has been chosen; a push by itself does not prove that a deployment succeeded.

items: Include the project name, purpose, features, technology, prerequisites, and exact install, run, and verification commands.
Add screenshots or a demo when useful, but never expose secrets, private data, or live tokens in them.
Explain contribution, pull-request, and review expectations; link relevant docs and project contacts where useful.
Name a license only after it has actually been chosen and added to the repository; credit third-party material when needed.

For GitHub Pages, verify the configured publishing source or workflow, build output/artifact, base path, and deployment status. Do not assume every push automatically and successfully publishes the site.
Never place passwords, API tokens, or private keys in the README, command examples, or screenshots.

blocks.text: Write readable documentation with Markdown

GitHub renders Markdown in README files, pull requests, issues, and other repository views. Use headings to express hierarchy, lists for related points, fenced code blocks for commands, and descriptive links for navigation. Preview the rendered result: Markdown characters that look correct in plain text can still produce a confusing page, and a link in a README does not verify that its destination exists.

blocks.code:

A short statement of the problem this project solves.

## Run locally
```bash

```

## Useful links
- [Source code](https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY)

steps.title: State the purpose
steps.explanation: A top-level heading names the project, and the short paragraph explains why a reader should care before they run commands.

steps.title: Fence command examples
steps.explanation: The second-level heading groups setup instructions. Triple backticks create a fenced code block; the bash label requests shell syntax highlighting and does not execute the commands.

steps.title: Use descriptive links
steps.explanation: Link text should describe the destination. Replace OWNER and REPOSITORY with the real path and open each link to confirm it works.

blocks.prompt: In a Markdown README, what do three backticks around commands usually create?

options.text: A fenced code block that preserves code formatting
options.feedback: Correct. The opening and closing fences separate code from prose; a language tag such as bash can enable syntax highlighting.

options.text: A heading whose level is selected automatically
options.feedback: Headings use leading hash marks such as # or ##, not code fences.

options.text: A terminal session that runs the commands on GitHub
options.feedback: Markdown displays commands as text. A reader must run them in the appropriate environment.

options.text: A deployment workflow that publishes the repository
options.feedback: A fenced block is only documentation; publishing must be configured separately.

blocks.explanation: Markdown formatting describes how repository text is rendered. It does not run shell commands or configure deployment.

blocks.text: Verify the GitHub Pages publishing path

GitHub Pages serves a static site from a configured publishing source or workflow. The fact that git push succeeded only proves that Git accepted the push; it does not prove that a build ran, an artifact was published, or the site deployment completed and is serving the new version. A project site may be served beneath a repository-name path, so the app's base path and asset URLs must match the published URL.

items: Open the repository's Settings → Pages and identify the actual publishing source: a selected branch/folder or GitHub Actions.
For a branch/folder source, confirm the selected branch and folder contain the intended static output. For an Actions source, inspect the workflow trigger, build command, artifact and deploy job.
Confirm the output includes the entry HTML and its required assets; verify the configured base path and links when the site is served below a repository-name path.
Check the latest deployment or Actions run, open the published URL, and test a representative route or asset.
If the site is stale or unavailable, inspect the failed deployment step and its logs instead of repeatedly pushing without diagnosing the cause.
Do not expect a static Pages deployment to provide a private server runtime. Never put secrets in client-side code or build output.

blocks.prompt: A push succeeded, but the GitHub Pages site still shows the previous version. What is the best first step?

options.text: Inspect the configured publishing source or deployment workflow, build output/base path, and latest deployment status
options.feedback: Correct. Deployment is a separate pipeline: confirm what is published and inspect the actual result and logs.

options.text: Keep pushing the same commit until the website updates
options.feedback: Repeated pushes do not diagnose a misconfigured source, failed build, wrong output directory, or base-path issue.

options.text: Delete .gitignore so all files are uploaded
options.feedback: .gitignore does not configure Pages deployment or select its publishing source.
Reset changes local repository state and does not fix the deployment configuration; it can also discard work.

blocks.explanation: A successful Git push and a successful website deployment are separate events. Verify the configured publishing path and the latest build/deploy evidence.

blocks.title: Prepare a README and verify a static-site deployment
blocks.context: You are preparing a small frontend repository for another developer and need to explain how to run it and how to check its published Pages site. The actual hosting configuration may use a branch/folder or a GitHub Actions workflow.

Add fenced setup and verification commands that match the repository's real package scripts.

Check the latest deployment or Actions run and note the evidence that the new version is available. If it failed, report the failed step rather than claiming success.

Do not invent a package command, Pages URL, publishing branch, or build directory.
Distinguish a successful push from a successful build and deployment.

blocks.text: Deep dive: Git's three areas and choosing a safe undo

Think of Git as separate snapshots and places where changes can live: the working tree contains your current edits, the index (staging area) records what the next commit will contain, and commits are saved snapshots connected by history. `git add` copies selected changes into the index; it does not commit them. Before undoing anything, inspect `git status` and `git diff` so you know which area contains the work.

blocks.code:
git status
git diff
git diff --staged
git add src/App.tsx
git diff --staged
git commit -m "fix: handle empty search results"
git log --oneline --decorate -5

steps.title: Inspect unstaged edits
steps.explanation: status shows the state of tracked/untracked files; diff shows edits in the working tree that are not staged.

steps.title: Inspect the proposed commit
steps.explanation: diff --staged shows the index—the exact content selected for the next commit. A file can contain both staged and unstaged changes at once.

steps.title: Create a snapshot only after review
steps.explanation: commit records the staged snapshot, and log helps confirm where HEAD now points. Commit messages should describe the intent, not just the file edited.

items: `git restore file` discards unstaged working-tree changes for that file; inspect them first because the discarded work may be hard to recover.
`git restore --staged file` removes a file from the index but keeps the working-tree edits.
`git revert <commit>` creates a new commit that reverses a previous commit; it is usually safer on shared branches.

`git reset` moves the current branch/HEAD and changes the index or working tree depending on flags; `--hard` discards tracked work and rewrites the branch position. Avoid it until you understand the target and have checked whether work is shared.

`git stash` temporarily shelves selected uncommitted changes; `git stash list` and `git stash apply` let you inspect/reapply them. `git reflog` can help find recent local HEAD positions after a mistaken reset, but it is not a substitute for remote backup.

blocks.title: Undo commands are not interchangeable
blocks.text: Use status/diff before changing state. For private, not-yet-committed work, restore or stash may fit. To undo a committed change already shared with the team, prefer revert unless your team explicitly coordinates history rewriting. Never run a destructive reset blindly to make a status screen look clean.

blocks.prompt: You pushed a commit to a shared feature branch and discover it introduced a bug. What is usually the safest undo approach?

options.text: Run git reset --hard HEAD~1 and force-push immediately
options.feedback: That rewrites shared history and may erase teammates' references or commits; it should not be done blindly.

options.text: Create a git revert commit for the bad commit
options.feedback: Revert records an inverse change as a new commit, preserving published history and making the correction visible to collaborators.
This destroys local repository metadata and does not safely undo a shared remote commit.

options.text: Run git restore on the repository root
options.feedback: Restore works on working-tree/index paths; it does not reverse a commit already published to the remote.

blocks.explanation: Choose the undo operation by identifying where the change lives and whether its history is shared.

blocks.text: Quick command reference: choose by intent

Use this as a lookup aid, not as a script to run blindly. Replace placeholders with real repository, branch, and commit names. Inspect status first, verify the remote destination before publishing, and follow the repository's pull-request and branch-protection rules. Fetch retrieves remote references; pull also attempts to integrate one into the current branch.

items: Start from a remote repository: `git clone <repository-url>` creates a local copy and configures the remote, commonly named `origin`.
Inspect your local state: `git status -sb` shows concise status and branch information; `git branch -vv` shows upstream tracking; `git remote -v` lists remote URLs.
Create a separate feature branch: `git switch -c feat/lesson-summary` creates and switches to a branch from the current commit. Start from the agreed, up-to-date base.

List and remove local branches: `git branch` lists them; after a branch has been merged, `git branch -d <branch>` removes it locally. Git refuses to delete an unmerged branch by default; do not use `-D` casually.

Merge a feature branch into the current target: `git merge <branch>` integrates the named branch into the checked-out branch. In a shared repository, follow the pull-request policy instead of merging directly into a protected branch.
Review the proposed commit: `git diff` displays unstaged edits; `git diff --staged` displays the content selected for the next commit.
Fetch without integrating: `git fetch origin` updates remote-tracking references without changing the current branch or working-tree files.

Integrate upstream only when fast-forward is possible: `git pull --ff-only` fetches and advances the current branch if it has no local divergence. It fails instead of inventing a merge when histories have diverged.

Publish the current branch: `git push -u origin HEAD` publishes the checked-out branch under the same name and configures upstream. It does not mean `main` unless you are on `main`; follow pull-request and branch-protection rules.
Undo a commit that was already shared: `git revert <commit>` adds an inverse commit and preserves the existing shared history.

blocks.prompt: You want to inspect newly published remote commits before deciding how to integrate them, without changing the current branch or working tree. Which command fits?

options.feedback: Fetch updates remote-tracking references but does not integrate their commits into the current branch.
Pull fetches and then attempts to integrate changes into the current branch when a fast-forward is possible.
This changes the current branch/worktree state and can discard tracked work; it is not an inspection-only operation.
Push publishes local commits to a remote; it does not retrieve newly published commits.

blocks.explanation: Choose a command based on which repository state it changes: fetch retrieves remote references; pull also integrates them, and reset can move local state destructively.
